title: Hilbert's 17th Problem — Historical Introduction
content: The module docstring traces the full history of Hilbert's 17th Problem. In 1888, Hilbert proved non-constructively that non-negative polynomials need not be sums of squares of polynomials. In 1900, he posed Problem 17: are they at least sums of squares of rational functions? Artin answered affirmatively in 1927 using real closed field theory and model-theoretic transfer. Motzkin (1967) gave the first explicit non-SOS polynomial. The file also explains why rational functions are necessary: the degree structure of leading forms in certain PSD polynomials prevents polynomial SOS decomposition.
mathContext: The question is: if $f \in \mathbb{R}[X_1, \ldots, X_n]$ and $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, does $f = \sum_i g_i^2$ for some $g_i \in \mathbb{R}(X_1, \ldots, X_n)$? Artin proved yes. The distinction between $\mathbb{R}[X]$ (polynomials) and $\mathbb{R}(X)$ (rational functions) is crucial.

title: SOS and PSD Definitions
content: Defines three flavors of sum-of-squares: IsSumOfSquaresPolynomial for univariate polynomial SOS, IsSumOfSquaresMvPolynomial for multivariate polynomial SOS, and IsSumOfSquaresRatFunc for rational function SOS. Each uses existential quantification over a finite list (Fin m → ...) of squared terms. Also defines IsPositiveSemidefinite (univariate) and IsPositiveSemidefiniteMv (multivariate) as non-negativity for all real inputs.
mathContext: A polynomial $p$ is SOS if $p = \sum_{i=1}^m q_i^2$. The key question: must $q_i \in \mathbb{R}[X]$ (polynomials) or can they be $q_i \in \mathbb{R}(X)$ (rational functions $g/h$)? PSD means $p(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$. The chain of implications is: polynomial-SOS $\Rightarrow$ rational-SOS $\Rightarrow$ PSD, and Artin proves PSD $\Rightarrow$ rational-SOS.

title: Artin's Theorem — The Main Result
content: The central theorem: every PSD multivariate polynomial over ℝ is a sum of squares of rational functions. The axiomatized statement uses algebraMap to embed the polynomial into the rational function field RatFunc. Artin's proof outline is documented: if p is not SOS in ℝ(X), an ordering of ℝ(X) making p negative exists; extending to the real closure gives a contradiction since p is non-negative at all real points. The univariate case is stated separately (artin_univariate) and is stronger: PSD univariate polynomials are actually polynomial-SOS.
mathContext: Artin's theorem: $\forall n, \forall p \in \mathbb{R}[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$, if $p(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, then $p = \sum_{i=1}^m g_i^2$ where $g_i \in \mathbb{R}(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$. The proof uses the Artin-Schreier theory of formally real fields: an element of a formally real field is a sum of squares iff it is positive in every ordering.

title: Motzkin's Counterexample
content: The Motzkin polynomial M(x,y) = x⁴y² + x²y⁴ - 3x²y² + 1 is defined as an MvPolynomial over Fin 2 and ℝ. Three key properties are established: (1) motzkin_nonneg proves M ≥ 0 everywhere via AM-GM (axiomatized), (2) motzkin_not_sos_polynomial proves M is not polynomial-SOS via degree analysis of the leading homogeneous form (axiomatized), and (3) motzkin_sos_ratfunc derives that M is rational-SOS by applying artin_hilbert17 — this is the only non-trivial deduction in the file, combining the non-negativity lemma with Artin's theorem.
mathContext: The AM-GM proof: $(x^4y^2 + x^2y^4 + 1)/3 \geq \sqrt[3]{x^4y^2 \cdot x^2y^4 \cdot 1} = x^2y^2$, so $M \geq 0$. The non-SOS proof: $M$ has degree 6, so any SOS decomposition requires degree-3 polynomials, but the leading form $x^4y^2 + x^2y^4 = x^2y^2(x^2+y^2)$ cannot be a sum of squares of degree-3 homogeneous polynomials in 2 variables.

title: Hilbert's 1888 Classification: When PSD = Polynomial-SOS
content: Hilbert (1888) completely classified when PSD implies polynomial-SOS: it holds if and only if (1) n = 1 (univariate, any degree), (2) d = 2 (quadratic forms, any number of variables), or (3) n = 2 and d = 4 (bivariate quartics). Two cases are axiomatized: univariate_psd_is_sos (using complex factorization: real roots have even multiplicity, complex roots come in conjugate pairs) and quadratic_psd_is_sos (using the Gram matrix / Cholesky decomposition: Q(x) = x^T A x with A ≽ 0 implies A = B^T B).
mathContext: Hilbert's classification: PSD = polynomial-SOS iff $(n, 2d) \in \{(n, 2) : n \geq 1\} \cup \{(1, 2d) : d \geq 1\} \cup \{(2, 4)\}$. The univariate proof uses $p(x) = c \prod (x - r_i)^{2e_i} \prod ((x-a_j)^2 + b_j^2)$ with $c > 0$, giving $p = q_1^2 + q_2^2$. The quadratic case uses $Q(x) = x^T A x$ with $A = L^T L$ (Cholesky), so $Q = \|Lx\|^2$.

title: Pfister's Bound on Number of Squares
content: Pfister (1967) proved that at most 2^n squares suffice to represent any n-variable PSD polynomial as a sum of squares of rational functions. The bound is optimal in general. The theorem is stated using Fin (2^n) to index the squares. Cassels' bound for the bivariate case (n = 2, so 4 squares) is stated separately. Both are axiomatized, with proofs requiring the theory of Pfister forms — multiplicative quadratic forms that arise from tensor products of binary forms.
mathContext: Pfister's theorem: if $p \in \mathbb{R}[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$ is PSD, then $p = \sum_{i=1}^{2^n} g_i^2$ with $g_i \in \mathbb{R}(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$. A Pfister form is a tensor product $\langle 1, a_1 \rangle \otimes \cdots \otimes \langle 1, a_n \rangle$, a $2^n$-dimensional quadratic form that is multiplicative. Cassels showed the bound $2^n$ is tight for $n = 2$.

title: Real Closed Fields and Transfer Principle
content: Explains the role of real closed fields in Artin's proof. A field R is real closed if it is formally real (−1 is not a sum of squares) and has no proper formally real algebraic extension. Equivalently: every positive element is a square, every odd-degree polynomial has a root, and the algebraic closure has degree 2. The transfer principle (real_closed_transfer) states that first-order statements about polynomial inequalities transfer between real closed fields. real_is_real_closed is a placeholder (True) for the fact that ℝ is real closed.
mathContext: A real closed field $R$ satisfies: (1) $-1 \notin \Sigma R^2$, (2) $R$ has no proper formally real algebraic extension. The Tarski-Seidenberg transfer principle: if $\varphi$ is a first-order sentence in the language of ordered fields, then $\varphi$ holds in $\mathbb{R}$ iff it holds in every real closed field. This is the model-theoretic core of Artin's proof.

title: Modern Applications: SOS Programming
content: Documents the modern computational significance of Hilbert 17. If a polynomial is polynomial-SOS, the decomposition can be found via semidefinite programming (SDP) in polynomial time. Applications include control theory verification, robotics safety certificates, and program invariant generation. The Positivstellensatz generalizes SOS certificates to constrained settings. Motzkin's counterexample explains the fundamental limitation: not all PSD polynomials admit polynomial-SOS certificates, so SDP-based methods are incomplete.
mathContext: SOS programming: find $p = \sum q_i^2$ by writing $p(x) = x_{\text{mon}}^T Q \, x_{\text{mon}}$ where $x_{\text{mon}}$ is the monomial vector and $Q \succeq 0$. This is a semidefinite program. The Positivstellensatz: if $\{g_i(x) \geq 0\}$ is infeasible over $\mathbb{R}^n$, there exist SOS certificates $s_j$ such that $-1 = s_0 + \sum s_j \prod g_{i_j}$.

title: Additional Counterexamples: Robinson and Choi-Lam
content: Two more PSD non-SOS polynomials are formalized. Robinson's polynomial R(x,y,z) = x⁶ + y⁶ + z⁶ - (symmetric cross terms) + 3x²y²z² is a 3-variable degree-6 example. Its non-negativity and non-SOS properties are axiomatized. The Choi-Lam polynomial CL(w,x,y,z) = w⁴ + x²y² + y²z² + z²w² - 4wxyz is a 4-variable degree-4 example (defined but properties not axiomatized). These show the phenomenon is pervasive beyond Motzkin's example.
mathContext: Robinson: $R(x,y,z) = \sum x_i^6 - \sum x_i^4 x_j^2 + 3x_1^2 x_2^2 x_3^2 \geq 0$ by Schur's inequality. Choi-Lam: $CL = w^4 + x^2y^2 + y^2z^2 + z^2w^2 - 4wxyz \geq 0$ by AM-GM. Both are PSD but not polynomial-SOS, demonstrated by analyzing homogeneous components.

title: Summary and Problem Status
content: The summary section uses #check to verify the main theorems are well-formed, then provides a prose overview. The key results are: artin_hilbert17 (PSD → rational-SOS), motzkin_not_sos_polynomial (PSD ↛ polynomial-SOS), univariate_psd_is_sos (univariate PSD = polynomial-SOS), and pfister_bound (at most 2^n squares). The practical distinction matters: polynomial-SOS is computationally tractable via SDP, while rational-SOS always exists but is harder to compute.
mathContext: The complete picture: PSD $\Rightarrow$ rational-SOS (Artin) but PSD $\not\Rightarrow$ polynomial-SOS (Motzkin). Special cases where PSD = polynomial-SOS: univariate (any degree), quadratic forms (any variables), bivariate quartics. Quantitatively: $\leq 2^n$ squares suffice (Pfister).
